final_review.summary: The paper proposes a procedural-fairness framework for causal models, arguing that existing causal fairness constraints can inadvertently distort neutral data-generating components. It introduces reference points and value-instantiation rules over local causal modules to decouple objectionable components while preserving neutral mechanisms. The conceptual framing is interesting and the method is coherent under its assumptions, but the overall case is weakened by strong dependence on known causal and normative structure, limited sensitivity analysis, and largely illustrative empirical evidence without uncertainty estimates. The paper is well presented, but the soundness and empirical support are not strong enough for acceptance.

strengths.item: Offers a useful conceptual reframing of causal fairness around procedural fairness and preservation of neutral data-generating mechanisms.
Identifies “disguised procedural unfairness” as an important failure mode of fairness-constrained learning.
Provides a concrete framework using local causal modules, reference points, value instantiation, and topological aggregation.
The proposed method is internally coherent under the stated DAG and objectionable-component assumptions.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, with clear algorithms and informative captions.

weaknesses.item: The technical novelty is moderate; the framework resembles structured causal interventions or blocking of unfair causal pathways rather than a fundamentally new causal formalism.
The method relies heavily on strong prior assumptions, including a known causal graph, known parent sets, and a normative classification of objectionable versus neutral components.
The experiments are mostly illustrative and do not substantially test robustness to graph misspecification, objectionable-edge choices, local-module errors, or reference-point optimization choices.
Empirical results lack repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, standard errors, or significance tests.
The operational connection between maximizing reference points for least advantaged individuals and satisfying the full Rawlsian Difference Principle remains only partially justified.
Some key figures are crowded and difficult to inspect at normal zoom.

requested_changes.item: Add sensitivity analyses for causal graph misspecification, alternative objectionable-component selections, and local-module estimation errors.
Report repeated-run results with uncertainty estimates and statistical tests for the empirical comparisons.
Clarify the precise relationship between the reference-point optimization objective and the claimed procedural fairness principles, especially the Difference Principle.
Strengthen empirical validation beyond illustrative approval-rate changes, ideally with broader datasets or more realistic causal-structure uncertainty.
Improve the readability of dense figures, especially legends, tick labels, annotations, and color-dependent encodings.
